programme: No single carrying set explains all twelve factors together. The record splits into two disjoint, internally coherent programmes that do not connect to each other: (1) MUC1 + HEY1, a renal papillary-carcinoma epithelial/Notch axis (HEY1 as Notch-pathway effector implicated in DLL4-driven renal-cell metastasis, MUC1 as a mucin marker used in papillary renal neoplasm workup), and (2) PER2 + TEF (+ weakly TCF7L2), a peripheral circadian/PAR-bZIP transcriptional loop (TEF is a canonical activator of Per2 transcription) tied in the literature to sleep, depression and rhythm disturbance in Parkinson's. Nothing in the material ties cluster 1 to Parkinson's or cluster 2 to kidney papillary carcinoma, and the remaining seven factors (ZNF384, E2F8, HOXD10, HTATIP2, MIXL1, ZEB1, and the discordant STOX1) return no literature evidence for either disease and do not bridge the two clusters mechanistically.
role_in_a: Not established from this material as a single programme: MUC1/HEY1 are grounded in kidney papillary carcinoma epithelial biology (mucin expression, Notch-driven metastasis) but the circadian factors (PER2, TEF) carry no Open Targets association and no retrieved paper places them in this cancer.
role_in_b: PER2 and TEF are directly documented in Parkinson's disease as circadian-output genes affecting sleep and depressive symptoms; MUC1 and HEY1 carry no Open Targets association in Parkinson's and no retrieved paper places them there.
shared_axis: None can be constructed from the given evidence: the two diseases' strongest factors (MUC1/HEY1 for A, PER2/TEF for B) are each well grounded in only one disease and absent, by both Open Targets and retrieval, from the other, so no single documented or inferable mechanism spans the pair.
reasoning: Statistical concordance across patient-group comparisons (up to 82/126) does not resolve into a shared biological module here: the highest-supported factors split cleanly by disease of origin with no overlapping targets, no shared complex, and no cross-disease citation. Rule 5 applies directly — twelve co-listed factors forming two unconnected disease-specific clusters is not a mechanism, and forcing a narrative across them would misrepresent the record.
support: PMID 39491020, 35054482, 31135486 — place MUC1 in kidney papillary/renal carcinoma only. PMID 24931473 — places HEY1 in renal cell carcinoma (Notch/DLL4 metastasis) only. PMID 39062963, 36717479, 36813077 — place PER2 in Parkinson's disease circadian/rhythm biology only. PMID 41135742, 23138696, 22257907 — place TEF in Parkinson's disease sleep/depression symptomatology only. PMID 36869069, 26499758 — place TCF7L2 in Parkinson's disease via shared diabetes-risk loci only. None of these touch the other disease in the pair; no PMID bridges cluster 1 and cluster 2.
how_to_falsify: Profile PER2/TEF rhythmic (time-of-day) expression directly in kidney papillary tumor tissue and matched normal kidney; if it is rhythmic and altered in tumor versus normal in a way that tracks MUC1/HEY1 expression, that would establish the missing link this account currently lacks. Conversely, absence of any circadian-gene dysregulation in the tumor tissue, and absence of MUC1/HEY1 signal in PD blood/CSF cohorts, would confirm the two clusters are independent as this account concludes.
caveats: 126 patient-group comparisons but only 2 independent cohort pairs, so replication depth is modest relative to the comparison count. STOX1 is explicitly discordant and excluded from any supporting claim. The single-view exclusions (ERG, ZNF174, ZNF32, etc.) and tissue-generic exclusions (KLF6, ERG, PURA, TCF7, KLF2, STAT5B, EZH2, LITAF, JUN, EBF1, RUNX2, TFE3) show the ranking already screened out one-off and tissue-default drivers — the fact that a coherent joint story still cannot be built from what remains is informative, not an artifact of insufficient filtering. Blood (PD) versus kidney tumor (KIRP) tissue sourcing also means any apparent concordance reflects network structure similarity across sample types, not necessarily shared cell-autonomous biology.
